claim: Perisynaptic Schwann cells (PSCs) are specialized, non-myelinating, synaptic glia of the neuromuscular junction (NMJ).
source: Perisynaptic Schwann cells (PSCs) are specialized, non-myelinating, synaptic glia of the neuromuscular junction (NMJ), that participate in synapse development, function, maintenance, and repair.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about PSC classification and characteristics.

claim: PSCs participate in synapse development, function, maintenance, and repair.
source: Perisynaptic Schwann cells (PSCs) are specialized, non-myelinating, synaptic glia of the neuromuscular junction (NMJ), that participate in synapse development, function, maintenance, and repair.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research in the introduction section.

claim: The study of PSCs has relied on an anatomy-based approach due to the absence of cell-specific PSC molecular markers.
source: The study of PSCs has relied on an anatomy-based approach, as the identities of cell-specific PSC molecular markers have remained elusive.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation in the field that motivated the current study.

claim: The absence of cell-specific molecular markers has precluded the ability to isolate and genetically manipulate PSCs in a cell specific manner.
source: This limited approach has precluded our ability to isolate and genetically manipulate PSCs in a cell specific manner.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the lack of specific markers.

claim: Neuron-glia antigen 2 (NG2) is a unique molecular marker of S100β+ PSCs in skeletal muscle.
source: We have identified neuron-glia antigen 2 (NG2) as a unique molecular marker of S100β+ PSCs in skeletal muscle.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the results.

claim: NG2 is expressed in Schwann cells already associated with the NMJ, indicating that it is a marker of differentiated PSCs.
source: NG2 is expressed in Schwann cells already associated with the NMJ, indicating that it is a marker of differentiated PSCs.
evidence: This is supported by developmental time course data showing NG2 expression appears after PSCs arrive at the NMJ.

claim: PSCs have a unique molecular signature that includes genes known to play critical roles in PSCs and synapses.
source: Using a newly generated transgenic mouse in which PSCs are specifically labeled, we show that PSCs have a unique molecular signature that includes genes known to play critical roles in PSCs and synapses.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data comparing PSCs to other cell types.

claim: The neuromuscular junction (NMJ) is a tripartite synapse comprised of an α-motor neuron (the presynapse), extrafusal muscle fiber (the postsynapse), and specialized synaptic glia called perisynaptic Schwann cells (PSCs).
source: The neuromuscular junction (NMJ) is a tripartite synapse comprised of an α-motor neuron (the presynapse), extrafusal muscle fiber (the postsynapse), and specialized synaptic glia called perisynaptic Schwann cells (PSCs) or terminal Schwann cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NMJ structure.

claim: The NMJ's large size and accessibility has made it essential for discovering fundamental mechanisms of synaptic function.
source: Due to its large size and accessibility, extensive research of the NMJ has been essential to the discovery of the fundamental mechanisms that govern synaptic function, including the concepts of neurotransmitter release, quantal transmission, and active zones, among others (Katz and Miledi, 1967; Fatt and Katz, 1952; Sealock et al., 1989; Sobel et al., 1979; Sobel et al., 1977; Sanes and Lichtman, 1999; Darabid et al., 2014; Katz and Miledi, 1966; Robertson, 1956; Changeux et al., 1970; Godfrey et al., 1984; Jennings et al., 1993; Lwebuga-Mukasa et al., 1976; Nitkin et al., 1987; Porter and Froehner, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to historical research.

claim: The concept of glia that exist primarily to support synapse function has its origins at the NMJ.
source: Likewise, the concept of glia that exist primarily to support synapse function, and thus the realization that synapses are tripartite, has its origins at the NMJ (Robertson, 1956; Couteaux, 1960; Kang et al., 2007; Zuo et al., 2004; Griffin and Thompson, 2008; Boeke, 1949; Heuser and Reese, 1973; Miledi and Slater, 1968; Miledi and Slater, 1970; Peper et al., 1974; Astrow et al., 1994; Astrow et al., 1998; Reynolds and Woolf, 1992; Young et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical research.

claim: PSCs surround the NMJ where they are closely associated with its pre- and postsynaptic components.
source: PSCs surround the NMJ where they are closely associated with its pre- and postsynaptic components (Griffin and Thompson, 2008; Ko and Robitaille, 2015; Darabid et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Very little is known about the molecular composition of PSCs.
source: While great progress has been made in understanding the cellular and physiological characteristics of PSCs, very little is known about the molecular composition of these cells (Ko and Robitaille, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The absence of a cell-specific molecular marker has hindered examinations of PSC development, differentiation and turnover.
source: This has hindered examinations of the processes of PSC development, differentiation and turnover.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the lack of specific markers.

claim: Isolation and targeting of PSCs for interrogation of molecular function in vivo and in vitro has not been possible.
source: Additionally, isolation and targeting of PSCs for interrogation of molecular function in vivo and in vitro has not been possible.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation in the field.

claim: The discovery of markers specific to PSCs is necessary to advance understanding of PSCs and synaptic glia.
source: Therefore, the discovery of markers specific to PSCs is necessary to advance our understanding of PSCs, and synaptic glia in general, on multiple fronts.
evidence: This is stated as a logical conclusion from the identified limitations.

claim: A growing number of molecular markers that recognize subsets of glial cells throughout the nervous system have been identified.
source: A growing number of molecular markers that recognize subsets of glial cells throughout the nervous system have been identified (Jäkel and Dimou, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: PSCs can be identified by the combined expression of S100β and NG2 genes.
source: We have found that PSCs can be identified by the combined expression of the calcium-binding protein B (S100β) (Brockes et al., 1979; Perez and Moore, 1968) and neuron-glia antigen-2 (NG2) (Stallcup, 1981; Bergles et al., 2010) genes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: A transgenic mouse was created that enables visualization and isolation of PSCs in a cell specific manner.
source: We utilized this unique molecular fingerprint to create a transgenic mouse that enables visualization and isolation of PSCs in a cell specific manner.
evidence: This is supported by the description of the S100β-GFP;NG2-dsRed mouse line.

claim: NG2 has been found to be co-expressed with S100β in a subset of glial cells in the developing brain.
source: We focused on NG2 for the following reasons: 1) it has been found to be co-expressed with S100β, a classical marker of all Schwann cells, in a subset of glial cells in the developing brain (Matthias et al., 2003; Hachem et al., 2005; Vives et al., 2003; Moshrefi-Ravasdjani et al., 2017; Platel et al., 2009); 2) published data show that it is expressed in skeletal muscles and labels pericytes and neural progenitor cells (Birbrair et al., 2013a; Birbrair et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: NG2 is expressed in skeletal muscles and labels pericytes and neural progenitor cells.
source: We focused on NG2 for the following reasons: 1) it has been found to be co-expressed with S100β, a classical marker of all Schwann cells, in a subset of glial cells in the developing brain (Matthias et al., 2003; Hachem et al., 2005; Vives et al., 2003; Moshrefi-Ravasdjani et al., 2017; Platel et al., 2009); 2) published data show that it is expressed in skeletal muscles and labels pericytes and neural progenitor cells (Birbrair et al., 2013a; Birbrair et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Widespread distribution of NG2-dsRed positive cells was observed in the EDL muscle, including a distinct subset of cells located specifically at the NMJ with PSC-like morphology.
source: We observed widespread distribution of NG2-dsRed postive cells in the EDL muscle, including a distinct subset of cells located specifically at the NMJ and with a similar morphology as PSCs (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A select subset of glia positive for both S100β-GFP and NG2-dsRed are specifically located at the NMJ.
source: However, we found a select subset of glia positive for both S100β-GFP and NG2-dsRed specifically located at the NMJ (yellow cells in Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: PSCs are the only cells expressing both S100β-GFP and NG2-dsRed in skeletal muscles.
source: Based on the location and morphology of the cell body and its elaborations, we concluded that PSCs are the only cells expressing both S100β-GFP and NG2-dsRed in skeletal muscles.
evidence: This is concluded from microscopy data showing location and morphology.

claim: The same number of PSCs are present at NMJs in the EDL muscle of S100β-GFP and S100β-GFP;NG2-dsRed mice.
source: In healthy young adult muscle, we observed the same number of PSCs at NMJs in the EDL muscle of S100β-GFP and S100β-GFP;NG2-dsRed mice (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The morphology of PSCs is indistinguishable between S100β-GFP and S100β-GFP;NG2-dsRed transgenic lines.
source: The morphology of PSCs also appeared to be indistinguishable between the two transgenic lines.
evidence: This is based on visual inspection of microscopy images.

claim: NMJ morphology, as assessed by fragmentation of nAChR clusters, is unchanged in S100β-GFP;NG2-dsRed mice compared to S100β-GFP and wild type mice.
source: In addition, the morphology of NMJs, as assessed by fragmentation of nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) clusters, is unchanged in S100β-GFP;NG2-dsRed mice compared to S100β-GFP and wild type mice (Figure 2A,B,D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The co-expression of S100β-GFP and NG2-dsRed does not appear to cause apparent deleterious changes on either PSCs or the postsynaptic region revealed by nAChRs.
source: Thus, the co-expression of S100β-GFP and NG2-dsRed does not appear to cause apparent deleterious changes on either PSCs or the postsynaptic region revealed by nAChRs.
evidence: This is concluded from the data showing no changes in PSC number or NMJ morphology.

claim: S100β-GFP;NG2-dsRed mice are outwardly indistinguishable when compared to S100β-GFP and wild type mice.
source: If so, we hypothesize that such changes would be minor given that S100β-GFP;NG2-dsRed mice are outwardly indistinguishable when compared to S100β-GFP and wild type mice.
evidence: This is an observation about the overall phenotype of the mice.

claim: NG2-dsRed and S100β-GFP are co-expressed exclusively in PSCs at 4d and 7d post-fibular nerve crush injury.
source: Similar to healthy uninjured EDL muscles (Figure 2E), NG2-dsRed and S100β-GFP were found co-expressed exclusively in PSCs at 4d and 7d post-injury (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figures 2F-G.

claim: Motor axons completely retract within 1 day and return to reinnervate vacated postsynaptic sites by 7 days post-fibular nerve crush in young adult mice.
source: In this injury model, motor axons completely retract within 1 day and return to reinnervate vacated postsynaptic sites by 7 days post-injury in young adult mice.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research on this injury model.

claim: NG2-dsRed and S100β-GFP are co-expressed only in PSCs in the EDL of P120 SOD1G93A;S100β-GFP;NG2-dsRed mice.
source: We again found NG2-dsRed and S100β-GFP co-expressed only in PSCs in the EDL of P120 SOD1G93A;S100β-GFP;NG2-dsRed mice (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The SOD1G93A mouse model exhibits significant degeneration of NMJs.
source: Second, we crossed the SOD1G93A mouse line, (Gurney et al., 1994) a model of ALS shown to exhibit significant degeneration of NMJs (Moloney et al., 2014), with S100β-GFP;NG2-dsRed mice and examined the expression pattern of NG2-dsRed and S100β-GFP in the EDL during the symptomatic stage (P120).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: S100β-GFP+ cells are present at the NMJ as early as embryonic day 15 (E15).
source: We observed the presence of S100β-GFP+ cells at the NMJ as early as embryonic day 15 (E15) with 100% of NMJs having at least one S100β-GFP+ cell by post-natal day 9 (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by developmental time course data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: 100% of NMJs have at least one S100β-GFP+ cell by post-natal day 9.
source: We observed the presence of S100β-GFP+ cells at the NMJ as early as embryonic day 15 (E15) with 100% of NMJs having at least one S100β-GFP+ cell by post-natal day 9 (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: During embryonic developmental stages, NMJs are exclusively populated by S100β-GFP+ cells that do not express NG2-dsRed.
source: During the embryonic developmental stages, we observed that NMJs are exclusively populated by S100β-GFP+ cells that do not express NG2-dsRed (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by developmental time course data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: At post-natal day 0 (P0), NG2-dsRed expression is observed in a small subset of S100β-GFP+ cells.
source: At post-natal day 0 (P0), however, we observed NG2-dsRed expression in a small subset of S100β-GFP+ cells (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This is supported by developmental time course data shown in Figure 3A and 3C.

claim: The proportion of NMJs with S100β-GFP+;NG2-dsRed+ cells sharply increased between P0 and P9, coinciding with the period of NMJ maturation in mouse skeletal muscles.
source: Notably, the proportion of NMJs with S100β-GFP+;NG2-dsRed+ cells sharply increased between the ages of P0 and P9, coinciding with the period of NMJ maturation in mouse skeletal muscles (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by developmental time course data shown in Figure 3C and a citation about NMJ maturation timing.

claim: By P21, when NMJ maturation in mice is near completion, S100β-GFP+;NG2-dsRed+ cells are exclusively present at NMJs.
source: By P21, when NMJ maturation in mice is near completion (Sanes and Lichtman, 1999), we observed S100β-GFP+;NG2-dsRed+ cells to be exclusively present at NMJs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by developmental time course data shown in Figure 3C and a citation about NMJ maturation timing.

claim: At P21, the number of S100β-GFP+;NG2-dsRed+ PSCs reached an average of 2.3 per NMJ and this remained unchanged in healthy young adult mice.
source: At this age, the number of S100β-GFP+;NG2-dsRed+ PSCs reached an average of 2.3 per NMJ and this remained unchanged in healthy young adult mice (Figure 3A,D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: NG2 protein is present at mature NMJs but not in NMJs of E18 mice.
source: We found NG2 protein present at mature NMJs but not in NMJs of E18 mice with IHC (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The induced expression of NG2 during NMJ development in Schwann cells located proximally to the NMJ provides evidence that NG2 is a marker of mature, differentiated S100β+ PSCs.
source: Thus, the induced expression of NG2 during the course of NMJ development in Schwann cells located proximally to the NMJ provides further evidence that NG2 is a marker of mature, differentiated S100β+ PSCs.
evidence: This is concluded from the developmental time course data.

claim: PSCs may upregulate NG2 during development to restrict motor axon growth at the NMJ.
source: It is possible that PSCs upregulate NG2 during development in order to restrict motor axon growth at the NMJ (Filous et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation based on known functions of NG2 in other contexts, supported by a citation.

claim: The constant presence of S100β-GFP+ cells and absence of single labeled NG2-dsRed+ cells at NMJs at every observed developmental time point strongly support that PSCs originate from Schwann cells.
source: Induced NG2 expression during NMJ development along with the constant presence of S100β-GFP+ cells (S100β-GFP+ or S100β-GFP+;NG2-dsRed+) and absence of single labeled NG2-dsRed+ cells at NMJs at every observed developmental time point (Figure 3B,C) strongly support previous studies indicating that PSCs originate from Schwann cells (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by developmental time course data shown in Figure 3B-C and a citation to prior research.

claim: PSC density is similar across EDL, soleus, and diaphragm muscles.
source: Here, we observed similar PSC densities in each muscle type (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the number of PSCs directly correlates with the size of the NMJ and not the functional characteristics or fiber type composition of the muscles with which they are associated.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The number of PSCs directly correlates with the size of the NMJ and not the functional characteristics or fiber type composition of the muscles.
source: Here, we observed similar PSC densities in each muscle type (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the number of PSCs directly correlates with the size of the NMJ and not the functional characteristics or fiber type composition of the muscles with which they are associated.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of similar PSC densities across different muscle types.

claim: The spacing of PSCs yielded high NNRI values and maintained ordered, non-random distributions at NMJs in the EDL muscle of adult mice.
source: We found that the spacing of PSCs yielded high NNRI values and thus maintained ordered, non-random distributions at NMJs in the EDL muscle of adult mice.
evidence: This is supported by nearest neighbor analysis data.

claim: The ordered distribution of PSCs is maintained regardless of the overall number of PSCs at a given NMJ.
source: Moreover, this ordered distribution was maintained regardless of the overall number of PSCs at a given NMJ (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is supported by nearest neighbor analysis data shown in Figure 4B-D.

claim: PSCs occupy distinct territories at adult NMJs.
source: These observations are in accord with a published study indicating that PSCs occupy distinct territories at adult NMJs (Brill et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research and is consistent with the current study's findings.

claim: Presynaptic, postsynaptic, and/or PSC-PSC mechanisms of communication dictate the spatial distribution of PSCs.
source: In addition, these data strongly suggest that presynaptic, postsynaptic, and/or PSC-PSC mechanisms of communication dictate the spatial distribution of PSCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of ordered PSC distribution.

claim: 567 genes enriched in PSCs were not previously recognized to be associated with PSCs, glial cells or synapses.
source: Notably, we found 567 genes enriched in PSCs that were not previously recognized to be associated with PSCs, glial cells or synapses (Supplementary file 1) using Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: A number of genes preferentially expressed by PSCs have known roles at synapses.
source: We also found a number of genes preferentially expressed by PSCs with known roles at synapses (Mozer and Sandstrom, 2012; Fox and Umemori, 2006; Rafuse et al., 2000; Ranaivoson et al., 2019; Shapiro et al., 2007; Peng et al., 2010; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and citations to prior research.

claim: Synaptogenesis, glutamate receptor, and axon guidance signaling are top canonical pathways under transcriptional regulation in PSCs.
source: Providing additional insights about the function of PSCs, IPA revealed synaptogenesis, glutamate receptor, and axon guidance signaling as top canonical pathways under transcriptional regulation (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: 27 genes expressed in isolated S100β-GFP+;NG2-dsRed+ PSCs were previously shown to be associated with PSCs.
source: This analysis identified 27 genes expressed in isolated S100β-GFP+;NG2-dsRed+ PSCs that were previously shown to be associated with PSCs (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data cross-referenced with published literature, shown in Table 1.

claim: PSCs express genes involved in detection and modulation of synaptic activity including adenosine, P2Y, acetylcholine and glutamate receptors, BChE, and L-type calcium channels.
source: These included genes involved in detection and modulation of synaptic activity such as adenosine (Robitaille, 1995; Rochon et al., 2001), P2Y (Robitaille, 1995; Heredia et al., 2018; Darabid et al., 2018), acetylcholine (Robitaille et al., 1997; Petrov et al., 2014; Wright et al., 2009) and glutamate receptors (Pinard et al., 2003), Butyrylcholinesterase (BChE) (Petrov et al., 2014), and L-type calcium channels (Robitaille et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and citations to prior research.

claim: PSCs express genes involved in NMJ development, synaptic pruning, and maintenance including agrin, CNP, Erbb2, Erbb3, Gab1, MAG, and Mpz.
source: Additionally, genes involved in NMJ development, synaptic pruning, and maintenance including agrin, 2',3'-cyclic nucleotide 3' phosphodiesterase (CNP) (Georgiou and Charlton, 1999), Erb-b2 receptor tyrosine kinase 2 (Erbb2) (Trachtenberg and Thompson, 1996; Morris et al., 1999; Woldeyesus et al., 1999), Erbb3 (Trachtenberg and Thompson, 1996; Riethmacher et al., 1997) GRB2-associated protein 1 (Gab1) (Park et al., 2017), myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG) (Georgiou and Charlton, 1999), and myelin protein zero (Mpz) (Georgiou and Charlton, 1999) were detected in PSCs.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and citations to prior research.

claim: qPCR analysis showed that eight genes (Ajap1, Col20a1, FoxD3, Nrxn1, PDGFa, Pdlim4, BChE, and NCAM1) are highly enriched in PSCs compared to all other cell types isolated via FACS.
source: Validating RNA-Seq findings, qPCR analysis showed that all eight genes are highly enriched in PSCs compared to all other cell types isolated via FACS (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Immunostaining showed that NG2 is concentrated at the NMJ.
source: Additionally, immunostaining showed that NG2, a novel PSC-enriched gene identified by RNA-Seq, is concentrated at the NMJ (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: NG2 is specifically expressed by S100β-GFP+ PSCs but not myelinating S100β-GFP+ Schwann cells.
source: We have shown that NG2 is specifically expressed by S100β-GFP+ PSCs but not myelinating S100β-GFP+ Schwann cells and thus the combined expression of S100β and NG2 is a unique molecular marker of PSCs in skeletal muscle.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy and RNA-seq data showing NG2 expression only in PSCs.

claim: Schwann cells induce expression of NG2 shortly after they arrive at the NMJ during maturation of the synapse.
source: Providing further evidence that NG2 is a marker of differentiated PSCs, we have demonstrated that Schwann cells induce expression of NG2 shortly after they arrive at the NMJ during maturation of the synapse.
evidence: This is supported by developmental time course data.

claim: This is the first time that the transcriptome of PSCs, or any other type of glial cell that associates exclusively with synapses, has been characterized.
source: To our knowledge this is the first time that the transcriptome of PSCs, or any other type of glial cell that associates exclusively with synapses, has been characterized.
evidence: This is stated as a novel contribution of the study.

claim: The analysis reveals expression of genes previously implicated in modulation of synaptic activity, synaptic pruning, and synaptic maintenance by PSCs.
source: This analysis reveals expression of a number of genes that have been previously implicated in modulation of synaptic activity, synaptic pruning, and synaptic maintenance by PSCs.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data cross-referenced with published literature.

claim: Novel genes highly expressed in PSCs but not Schwann cells or NG2+ cells were identified.
source: We identified a number of novel genes that are highly expressed in PSCs but not Schwann cells or NG2+ cells.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: The identified genes have the potential to serve as molecular markers for PSC-specific genetic manipulations, PSC ablation, and isolation of PSCs for cell culture and molecular analysis.
source: These genes have the potential to assist PSC research by serving as molecular markers that can be utilized for PSC-specific genetic manipulations, PSC ablation, and isolation of PSCs for cell culture and molecular analysis.
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications of the findings.

claim: The analysis reveals a unique gene expression signature that distinguishes PSCs from all other Schwann cells.
source: This analysis, therefore, reveals a unique gene expression signature that distinguishes PSCs from all other Schwann cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the RNA-seq data showing differential gene expression.

claim: Many genes enriched in PSCs have been shown to play key roles in neuronal circuits in the central nervous system and in cell-cell communication.
source: While the role of the majority of genes found enriched in PSCs at the neuromuscular synapse remains to be determined, it is worth noting that many have been shown to play key roles in neuronal circuits in the central nervous system and in cell-cell communication.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of gene functions from other contexts.

claim: NG2 has been shown to terminate axonal growth in glial scars in the spinal cord.
source: This is the case for NG2 which has been shown to terminate axonal growth in glial scars in the spinal cord (Filous et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: NG2 may be utilized by PSCs to tile and occupy unique territories, and prevent motor axons from developing sprouts that extend beyond the postsynaptic partner.
source: Therefore, it is possible that NG2 is utilized by PSCs to tile, and thus occupy unique territories, and prevent motor axons from developing sprouts that extend beyond the postsynaptic partner.
evidence: This is speculation based on known functions of NG2 in other contexts.

claim: The NG2 promoter is active in some PSCs at P0, a time when motor axon nerve endings at NMJs undergo rapid morphological changes.
source: Supporting this possibility, we have found that the NG2 promoter is active in some PSCs at P0 (Figure 3C), a time when motor axon nerve endings at NMJs undergo rapid morphological changes (Sanes and Lichtman, 1999; Sanes and Lichtman, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by developmental time course data shown in Figure 3C and citations about NMJ development.

claim: The progressive activation of the NG2 promoter in PSCs is complete by P9, which coincides with the elimination of extranumeral axons innervating the same postsynaptic site in mice.
source: The progressive activation of the NG2 promoter in PSCs is complete by P9 (Figure 3C), which coincides with the elimination of extranumeral axons innervating the same postsynaptic site in mice (Sanes and Lichtman, 1999; Sanes and Lichtman, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by developmental time course data shown in Figure 3C and citations about NMJ development.

claim: PSCs may utilize NG2 to promote the maturation of the presynaptic region and thus the NMJ.
source: Therefore, PSCs may utilize NG2 to promote the maturation of the presynaptic region and thus the NMJ.
evidence: This is speculation based on the timing of NG2 expression during development.

claim: PSCs may utilize NG2 to repel each other as they tile during development to occupy unique territories at the NMJ.
source: Furthermore, PSCs may utilize NG2 to repel each other as they tile during development to occupy unique territories at the NMJ (Brill et al., 2011).
evidence: This is speculation based on known functions of NG2 and observations of PSC tiling, supported by a citation.

claim: The tools developed allow determination of which cellular and molecular determinants are critical for PSC differentiation, maturation, and function at the NMJ.
source: With these tools, it is now possible to determine which cellular and molecular determinants are critical for PSC differentiation, maturation, and function at the NMJ.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application of the developed tools.

claim: The tools will allow ascertainment of the contribution of PSCs to NMJ repair following injury and NMJ degeneration during normal aging and neuromuscular diseases.
source: It will also allow us to ascertain the contribution of PSCs to NMJ repair following injury and NMJ degeneration during normal aging and the progression of neuromuscular diseases, such as Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) and Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA).
evidence: This is stated as a potential application of the developed tools.

claim: The strategy of specifically labeling synaptic glia using a combination of protein markers may serve as a springboard for studying synapse-associated glia throughout the CNS.
source: Our strategy of specifically labeling synaptic glia, using a combination of protein markers uniquely expressed in this cell type, may serve as a springboard for unprecedented approaches for studying not only PSC function at the NMJ, but also synapse-associated glia throughout the CNS.
evidence: This is speculation about broader applications of the approach.

claim: Subsets of astrocytes in the brain co-express both S100β and NG2.
source: Indeed, we have observed subsets of astrocytes in the brain that co-express both S100β and NG2, as has been previously reported in the context of a lineage tracing analysis (Deloulme et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by observations in the current study and a citation to prior research.

claim: S100β is a classical marker of all Schwann cells.
source: We focused on NG2 for the following reasons: 1) it has been found to be co-expressed with S100β, a classical marker of all Schwann cells, in a subset of glial cells in the developing brain (Matthias et al., 2003; Hachem et al., 2005; Vives et al., 2003; Moshrefi-Ravasdjani et al., 2017; Platel et al., 2009); 2) published data show that it is expressed in skeletal muscles and labels pericytes and neural progenitor cells (Birbrair et al., 2013a; Birbrair et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is established knowledge about S100β.

claim: In the S100β-GFP mouse line, the S100β promoter drives expression of GFP in all Schwann cells.
source: To determine if NG2 is expressed in PSCs we generated a transgenic mouse line (referred herein as S100β-GFP;NG2-dsRed; Figure 1A) by crossing the NG2-dsRed line with the S100β-GFP mouse line in which the S100β promoter drives expression of GFP in all Schwann cells (Zuo et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation describing the S100β-GFP mouse line.

claim: In S100β-GFP;NG2-dsRed double transgenic mice, dsRed labels all NG2 positive cells and GFP labels all Schwann cells in skeletal muscles.
source: As expected, in the resulting S100β-GFP;NG2-dsRed double transgenic mouse line, dsRed labeled all NG2 positive cells (referred herein as NG2-dsRed+) and GFP labeled all Schwann cells (referred herein as S100β-GFP+) (Figure 1B–C) in skeletal muscles.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: At non-synaptic sites in skeletal muscle, GFP-positive cells do not express dsRed and dsRed-positive cells do not express GFP.
